lesson.title: Flat Lines: Understanding Zero Slope
lesson.summary: A slope of exactly zero describes a perfectly flat, horizontal line where the output never changes no matter how the input changes.
lesson.body:
Slope measures rise over run, and there is nothing stopping the rise from being 0 while the run is some nonzero number. When that happens, the slope itself equals 0, because 0 divided by any nonzero number is still 0. A line with 0 slope is perfectly flat: it neither climbs nor falls as you move along it from left to right. Every point on the line shares the exact same y-coordinate, even though the x-coordinate keeps changing.

Zero slope describes any situation where the output stays constant no matter what the input does. A thermostat holding a room at a fixed 68 degrees keeps that temperature whether 1 minute or 60 minutes pass. A flat, level stretch of road has the same elevation at every point along it. A subscription price that stays 12 dollars a month regardless of how many months pass is another example. In each case, changing the input produces no change at all in the output, which is the defining feature of 0 slope.

Take the points (2, 4) and (7, 4) and apply the slope formula. Here x1 = 2, y1 = 4, x2 = 7, y2 = 4, so m = (4 minus 4) divided by (7 minus 2), which is 0 divided by 5. Since the numerator is 0 and the denominator is a nonzero number, the entire fraction equals 0. The slope is exactly 0. Notice that the y-coordinates were identical, 4 and 4, at both points, while the x-coordinates were different, 2 and 7. Whenever the y-coordinates of two points match exactly, the line through them will always have 0 slope, since the rise in the numerator will always come out to 0.

It helps to keep 0 slope distinct from a small slope. A slope like 0.01 is very close to 0 and looks nearly flat on many graphs, but it is not actually 0, and the line will eventually rise or fall if you follow it far enough. True 0 slope means the rise is exactly 0 forever, not just small, so the line never changes height at all, no matter how far you travel along it in either direction. This distinction matters when you later write the equation of a line, because a genuinely flat line has an equation of the form y equals a constant, which you will study closely as a horizontal line.

Recognizing 0 slope quickly is straightforward: check whether the two given y-coordinates are the same number. If they are, you already know the slope is 0 before doing any division, since the rise between them has to be 0.

It is also worth testing 0 slope inside slope-intercept form to see why the x-term disappears. Starting from y equals mx plus b and substituting m = 0 gives y equals 0 times x plus b. Since 0 times any x-value is always 0, the equation simplifies to y equals b, with no x appearing at all. That is precisely why the equation of a perfectly flat line never contains x, and it previews the horizontal line equation you will study next, where a single constant tells you the entire graph. Contrast this with a line of a small but nonzero slope, such as 0.1, whose equation would be y equals 0.1x plus b: that line looks nearly flat over a short stretch of graph paper, but it is still technically climbing, and given enough horizontal distance it will rise by any amount you like, which a true 0 slope line, with its constant equation, never will.
